templates.pattern: A solar project has a base LCOE of £[LCOE_BASE]/MWh. A [DELTA]% increase in capital cost and a [CF_DROP]% reduction in capacity factor are modelled simultaneously. Calculate the new LCOE (£/MWh). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
New LCOE = Base LCOE × (1 + ΔCAPEX%) / (1 − ΔCF%)
= [LCOE_BASE] × (1 + [DELTA]/100) / (1 − [CF_DROP]/100)
= £[RESULT]/MWh

LCOE sensitivity analysis quantifies how robust a project is to cost overruns and resource variability. LCOE is directly proportional to capital cost and inversely proportional to energy yield. A combined 20% cost increase and 10% yield decrease can raise LCOE by ~33%, potentially making a project unviable.

templates.pattern: A downstream wind turbine is in the wake of an upstream turbine. The upstream turbine has power output [P1] kW. The wake reduces wind speed by [WD]% at the downstream rotor. Calculate the downstream turbine power (kW), noting that power ∝ v³. Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Since P ∝ v³:
P2 = P1 × (1 − WD/100)³
= [P1] × (1 − [WD]/100)³
= [RESULT] kW

Wake effects can reduce downstream turbine output by 10–40%. Wind farm layouts use turbine spacing of 5–10 rotor diameters to minimise wake losses. Wake models (Jensen, Gaussian) are used in wind farm optimisation software to maximise total array output.

templates.pattern: A fixed-tilt solar array generates [E_FIXED] MWh/yr. A single-axis tracking system increases energy yield by [GAIN]%. Calculate the additional energy generated (MWh/yr) and the total tracked yield (MWh/yr).
templates.explanation:
Tracked Yield = Fixed Yield × (1 + Gain%)
= [E_FIXED] × (1 + [GAIN]/100)
= [RESULT] MWh/yr

Additional energy = [RESULT] − [E_FIXED] = [RESULT-E_FIXED] MWh/yr

Single-axis (N–S axis) trackers boost yield 20–30% by following the sun's daily east–west arc. Dual-axis tracking adds a further 5–10% by also following seasonal N–S movement. The economic case depends on tracker cost vs. extra revenue from additional generation.

templates.pattern: An electrolyser produces hydrogen from water using [POWER] kW of electricity. Electrolyser efficiency is [EFF]% and the energy content of hydrogen (HHV) is 39.4 kWh/kg. Calculate the hydrogen production rate (kg/hr). Round to 4 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
H₂ Production Rate = (Power × Efficiency) ÷ Energy content of H₂
= ([POWER] × [EFF]/100) ÷ 39.4 kWh/kg
= [RESULT] kg/hr

Green hydrogen from renewable-powered electrolysis is central to decarbonising hard-to-electrify sectors (steel, shipping, fertilisers). PEM electrolysers achieve 70–80% efficiency; alkaline electrolysers 60–75%. The 39.4 kWh/kg figure uses the Higher Heating Value (HHV) of hydrogen.

templates.pattern: A pumped hydro storage system pumps [V] m³ of water uphill ([EFF_P]% pump efficiency) and generates electricity on discharge ([EFF_T]% turbine efficiency). Head h = [H] m, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Calculate the round-trip efficiency (%) and energy delivered (kWh). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Potential energy stored = ρ × g × V × h = 1000 × 9.81 × [V] × [H] J
Energy input (pumping) = PE / (η_pump) 
Energy output (generation) = PE × η_turbine
Energy delivered = ρgVh × η_pump × η_turbine ÷ 3,600,000 J/kWh
= [RESULT] kWh
Round-trip efficiency = [EFF_P]% × [EFF_T]% / 100 = [EFF_P*EFF_T/100]%

Pumped hydro provides ~95% of global grid-scale energy storage. Round-trip efficiency of 70–85% is much better than hydrogen (25–40%). It provides long-duration storage (hours to days) essential for balancing seasonal renewable variability.

templates.pattern: Grid frequency drops from 50 Hz to [FREQ] Hz following a generation trip. A battery storage system must inject [POWER] MW of frequency response power within 1 second. Calculate the energy dispatched (MWh) in a [DURATION] second response window. Round to 6 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Energy dispatched = Power × Time ÷ 3600 s/hr
= [POWER] MW × [DURATION] s ÷ 3600
= [RESULT] MWh

Frequency = [FREQ/100] Hz (deviation = [50 - FREQ/100] Hz from 50 Hz nominal).

Batteries are uniquely suited to grid frequency response due to sub-second response times. In Great Britain, frequency must stay within 49.5–50.5 Hz (normal) and 47–52 Hz (emergency). Battery storage providing Dynamic Containment services earns premium revenues for rapid frequency response.

templates.pattern: A renewable energy site is [DIST] km from the grid connection point. The transmission cable has a resistance of [R_PER_KM] ohms/km and carries [I] amps. Calculate the total transmission power loss (kW) and the loss as a percentage of the [GEN] MW generated. Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Total resistance R = R_per_km × Distance = [R_PER_KM] × [DIST] Ω
Transmission Loss = I² × R = [I]² × [R_PER_KM×DIST] W
= [RESULT] kW
Loss% = [RESULT] kW ÷ ([GEN]×1000 kW) × 100

Transmission losses increase with distance and resistance, and fall with higher voltage (lower current). HVDC cables are preferred for distances >80 km offshore because AC cables generate large reactive power losses at long distances, leaving less capacity for real power transmission.

templates.pattern: A wind farm generates [GEN] GWh of electricity in a year but [CURT] GWh is curtailed (wasted) due to grid constraints. Calculate the curtailment rate (%) and the actual energy exported to the grid (GWh). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Curtailment Rate = Curtailed Energy ÷ Total Generated Energy × 100
= [CURT] ÷ [GEN] × 100
= [RESULT]%
Energy exported = [GEN] − [CURT] = [GEN-CURT] GWh

Curtailment occurs when grid capacity is insufficient to absorb all generated power. In some markets (e.g., Texas, UK) curtailment rates of 5–15% are common. Solutions include grid reinforcement, demand-side response, battery storage, and interconnectors to neighbouring regions.

templates.pattern: A solar panel has an energy payback time of [EPBT] years and an operational lifetime of [LIFE] years. During operation it generates [EOUT] kWh/yr. Its manufacture required [EIN] kWh of primary energy. Calculate the Energy Payback Ratio (EPR = lifetime energy output ÷ energy input). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Energy Payback Ratio (EPR) = Lifetime Energy Output ÷ Energy Input
= ([EOUT] × [LIFE]) ÷ [EIN]
= [RESULT]

EPR > 1 confirms the panel is energy-positive over its lifetime. Typical crystalline silicon solar panels have EPR of 10–30× and EPBT of 1–3 years. Wind turbines have EPR of 20–80×. Higher EPR indicates a more energy-efficient investment in renewable infrastructure.

templates.pattern: A solar PV system has a total lifecycle CO₂ emissions of [LCA_CO2] tonnes from manufacture, installation, maintenance and decommissioning. Over its [LIFE]-year lifetime it generates [TOTAL_E] GWh of electricity. Calculate the lifecycle CO₂ intensity (gCO₂/kWh). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Lifecycle CO₂ Intensity = Total CO₂ ÷ Total Energy Generated
= [LCA_CO2] tonnes × 10⁶ g/tonne ÷ ([TOTAL_E] GWh × 10⁶ kWh/GWh)
= [RESULT] gCO₂/kWh

Life cycle CO₂ reference values (gCO₂/kWh): coal ~820, gas CCGT ~490, nuclear ~12, onshore wind ~7–11, solar PV ~20–50, offshore wind ~8–16. Even accounting for manufacturing emissions, renewables emit 20–100× less CO₂ per kWh than fossil fuels over their operational lifetime.
